title: dedicated-gpu-pool-scheduling-autoscale-warmup-debug-scratchpad-4
content:
Scratchpad: Dedicated GPU pool scheduling / autoscale warmup - capacity thrash
Owner: Evan Park (eng-serving-runtime)
Collaborators: Maya, Jasper
Dates: reproductions 2026-02-21 -> investigation notes 2026-02-25

Summary:
- Intermittent "capacity thrash" observed during scale-ups: new GPU nodes start but traffic keeps being routed to older nodes or to fallback models, causing repeated scale-up then scale-down cycles. Warmup appears incomplete leading to request errors or high tail latency.
- Symptoms seen in customer-prod dedicated pool (pool-id: pool-ded-nyc-3) during synthetic load tests and a couple customer spikes.

High-level hypothesis:
1) New pods/instances are marked Ready quickly by k8s (container up) but the model KV/cache warmup (disk->GPU load, quantized weights) completes later - upstream LB begins routing before kernel caches populated.
2) Autoscaler policy reacts to queued requests / high pending metrics and brings up nodes, but because warmup latency > scale decision window, autoscaler triggers additional nodes -> overshoot -> cooldown sees underutilization -> scale down -> repeat.
3) There may be a mismatch between pod readiness probe and actual serving readiness (no explicit readiness that waits for model load).
4) Cold-start init fails occasionally with transient OOMs (OOMKilled) during heavy concurrent model load causing pods to restart and increase thrash.

Commands/tests run (raw):
- kubectl get pods -n redwood-dedicated -l pool=pool-ded-nyc-3 -o wide
  => pods cycle through Running -> Ready quickly (container ready) but custom /health/serving returns 503 for 20-45s.

- kubectl logs -n redwood-dedicated pod/serve-xy-5f8 --since=1h | grep -i warmup
  => [2026-02-21T14:03:12Z] INFO model_warmup: starting weight load
     [2026-02-21T14:03:45Z] WARN gpu_mem: high-alloc during warmup (peak 28.9GB)
     [2026-02-21T14:04:05Z] INFO model_warmup: finished, kv-cache hits=0

- Prometheus queries (used grafana explore):
  - sum(rate(serving_request_queue_length[30s])) by (pool) spiked to 120 at 14:02
  - kube_pod_container_status_ready{pool="pool-ded-nyc-3"} shows 90% ready within 10s, but custom_metric_model_loaded{pod} shows 0->1 only after 35s.

- Autoscaler logs (controller) from cluster:
  - [14:02:12] scale-up(pool-ded-nyc-3): target=3 -> 6 (reacting to pending requests metric)
  - [14:02:50] scale-down(pool-ded-nyc-3): target=6 -> 2 (cooldown underutilization)
  - Note: scale decisions are 30s buckets, cooldown 60s - too aggressive for model warmup.

- Reproduced locally with load generator (k6): 100 rps burst for 45s -> observed identical oscillation.

Error snippets seen:
- 503 /health/serving (timeout) during warmup window
- 500 internal errors with stack: "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory while loading weights" (OOMKilled restarts in logs)
- client side: "request timed out after 15s" (some clients have 15s timeout; contributes to retries)

What we tried already:
1) Adjusted deployment readinessProbe to check /health/serving (calls model_ready flag) instead of container ready. Result: reduced early routing but not eliminated because readiness probe returned success before full kv-cache priming (probe threshold too loose).
2) Increased per-pod initResources CPU to 2 cores and memory to 36GB (from 24GB) in a canary pool - OOM frequency reduced but not eliminated for largest models (70B quantized).
3) Added a postStart hook to touch GPU memory mapping and run a minimal forward pass (single prompt) to force early kernel JIT. This helped reduce latency of first token from ~8s -> ~2s for small models, but larger models still hit peak allocations and sometimes OOM.
4) Tuned autoscaler scale-up step: limit max-step to +2 nodes per 30s (was +5) to reduce overshoot. This reduced oscillation amplitude but customer spikes still trip it.
5) Implemented a warmup-caching sidecar (in experiment) that prefetches quant files from PVC to local NVMe - small win on IO-bound startup but does not solve GPU mem allocation ordering.

Open questions / hypotheses to validate:
- Are we sequentially allocating weight blobs causing fragmentation? If model loader requests many allocations concurrently, fragmentation causes effective available GPU memory < model size -> OOM during warmup. Need to observe cudaMem info during load.
- Is there a kernel JIT or cuFFT step that is blocking and taking variable time per instance? Can we pre-JIT on one warm instance and snapshot?
- Should autoscaler use the custom_metric_model_loaded (binary per-pod) as a gating metric before routing traffic / counting pod capacity?
- Can we implement a "warmup grace" window in the routing layer (Keep new nodes out of LB until model_loaded metric true)?

Short-term mitigations (priority):
- Make readiness probe stricter: require model_loaded metric and a quick inference call to pass (integrated probe). Roll out to canary pool only.
- Autoscaler: add a soft gating condition that does not count pods as available until model_loaded==1; also reduce max-step during bursts.
- Client-side: increase retry/backoff heuristics and bump request timeouts to 30s for critical customers during rollout.

Longer-term fixes (research/engineering):
- Model loader improvements to allocate a single large contiguous allocation or use memory pooling to avoid fragmentation.
- Support pre-warm pool: keep N standby warmed instances per model for pools with strict latency SLO. Could be per-customer reserve.
- Kernel JIT snapshotting or early compile phase offload to a background precompiler.

Repro steps (clean):
1) Spin up a test dedicated pool with same node profile as prod: g4dn-like with 48GB GPU mem (quantized model profile settings).
2) Deploy serving runtime with current main branch + logging hooks enabled (enable model_loaded metric).
3) Run k6 scenario: 0->100rps ramp in 5s, sustain 60s, ramp down. Observe scale decisions and model_loaded timing.
4) Capture kube events + autoscaler controller logs + Prometheus scrape for custom metrics.

Next immediate tasks (todo):
- [ ] Add model_loaded to readiness probe on canary pool and monitor for 24h (Evan).
- [ ] Add gate in routing layer to exclude pods until model_loaded==1 (Maya) - design doc link in JIRA-1428.
- [ ] Add CUDA mem tracing during warmup to a debug-logging mode (Jasper) - short patch to export /metrics/cuda_mem_alloc attempts.
- [ ] Run 10 repeat burst reproductions and collect heap/gpu traces (Evan + Jasper).
- [ ] Evaluate whether reservation of small pre-warmed pool per hot-model is economical (calc expected $/hr vs tails).

Notes / oddities:
- Observed one pod where model_loaded==1 but first inference failed with CUDA kernel launch error; subsequent inferences succeeded. Looks like transient driver hiccup. Log snippet: "cuLaunchKernel failed: CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT" - need to check driver/kernel versions.
- Some customer traffic uses small prompt but multi-shot which causes short-lived high concurrency; batching behavior interacts with warmup (larger batches during warmup can spike memory).

Links / references:
- https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/456 (experimental readiness probe changes)
- JIRA-1428 (track: autoscale warmup gating)
- Slack thread: #dedicated-autoscale (pinned logs)

If we can agree on immediate canary changes (readiness gating + scale-step cap) we should be able to reduce thrash significantly and buy time to implement loader-level memory fixes and pre-warm pool support.

End of scratchpad.
